plan: Ten new items; every topic and choice set checked against the live bank (a restrictive-'that' punctuation item and a 'including' colon item were dropped as matching 127 and 092). anomalous/mundane WIC, hummingbird torpor purpose, naked mole-rat dialect inference, hand-hygiene observer data, nutcracker landmark hypothesis evidence, Stonehenge bluestones cross-text, Tu Youyou synthesis, concession transition, irregular past participle. Relabelled to the blind solvers' rating where it was lower: S037-01 medium→easy, S037-03 medium→easy, S037-04 hard→medium, S037-05 medium→easy, S037-06 hard→easy, S037-07 hard→easy, S037-08 medium→easy, S037-09 medium→easy.

passages.title: An odd reading
passages.text: Most of the probe's temperature readings fell within the range engineers had predicted, but one reading from the sensor near the antenna was so far outside that range that the team at first suspected a faulty instrument rather than a real change. Engineers called the reading ______ and scheduled a second measurement to check it.

passages.title: Ordinary objects
passages.text: The photographer is known for turning ______ subjects into striking images: a dish rack, a parking meter, and a puddle reflecting a streetlight have all appeared in her prize-winning series.

passages.title: Hummingbird nights
passages.text: Hummingbirds have the highest metabolism of any bird, and a hummingbird can burn through its energy reserves overnight if it stays fully active. On cold nights, many hummingbirds enter torpor, a sleeplike state in which body temperature can fall by many degrees and heart rate slows dramatically. In this state, a bird uses only a small fraction of the energy it would otherwise need. Researchers studying hummingbirds high in the Andes have recorded body temperatures during torpor as low as about 3 degrees Celsius.

passages.title: Mole-rat dialects
passages.text: Naked mole-rats live in underground colonies and greet one another with soft chirps. Researchers found that each colony's chirps share a distinct pattern, or dialect, and that mole-rats respond more strongly to chirps in their own colony's dialect. Pups moved to a different colony shortly after birth grew up producing the dialect of the colony that raised them, not the one they were born into. And when a colony's queen was removed, the colony's chirps became more varied, until a new queen took over and the calls grew similar again. These findings suggest that ______

passages.title: Watching hands
passages.text:
A hospital measured how often staff cleaned their hands when entering patients' rooms, using two methods over the same months.
Method | Hand-cleaning rate
Trained observer visibly present on the ward | 85%
Automated sensors, no observer present | 40%
Researchers concluded that rates recorded by visible observers likely overstate how often staff clean their hands when no one appears to be watching.

passages.title: Remembering caches
passages.text: Clark's nutcrackers bury thousands of pine seeds in the fall and recover many of them months later. Biologist Stephen Vander Wall hypothesized that the birds find their caches by remembering the positions of nearby landmarks, such as rocks and logs, rather than by smell or by searching at random.

passages.title: The bluestones (two texts)
passages.text:
Text 1
Some geologists have argued that the smaller "bluestones" at Stonehenge, which came from the Preseli Hills in Wales about 230 kilometers away, were carried most of the way to England by glaciers during an ice age, so that Stonehenge's builders had only to collect them nearby.
Text 2
Archaeologists led by Mike Parker Pearson excavated two outcrops in the Preseli Hills and found stone tools, wedges, and artificial platforms beneath the rock faces, along with hearths dated to around the time Stonehenge was built. They also found gaps in the outcrops that match the shapes of bluestones at Stonehenge.

passages.title: Tu Youyou
passages.text:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:
• In 1969, the Chinese scientist Tu Youyou began searching for a new malaria treatment.
• Her team screened more than 2,000 traditional herbal remedies.
• A 1,600-year-old text described soaking sweet wormwood in cold water.
• Following that clue, Tu extracted the plant at a low temperature, which preserved its active compound, artemisinin.
• In 2015, she shared the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for the discovery.

passages.title: A slow method
passages.text: Radiocarbon dating requires destroying a small sample of the object being tested, and results can take weeks to arrive. ______ the method remains the standard for dating organic material up to about 50,000 years old, because no other technique matches its accuracy across that span.

passages.title: A prolific director
passages.text: By the time the choir's founding director retired in 2019, she had ______ more than forty original pieces for the group, several of which are still performed every season.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.explanation: A reading that departs sharply from all the others and from predictions is "anomalous."

A.rationale: A reading so far outside the predicted range was not routine.

B.rationale: The team planned a second measurement to check it, so they did not consider it conclusive.

D.rationale: A reading unlike all the others does not merely repeat them.

hints: How did this reading compare with the others?
candidates.remember: Contrast with the other readings defines the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
candidates.evidence: a dish rack, a parking meter, and a puddle
candidates.explanation: The examples are everyday, unremarkable objects, so the photographer turns "mundane" subjects into striking images.

B.rationale: A dish rack and a parking meter are everyday objects, not exotic ones.

C.rationale: Nothing suggests the subjects cause disagreement.

D.rationale: The examples are modern, everyday objects.

hints: What do the examples have in common?
candidates.remember: Examples after a colon define the blank.

candidates.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To argue that hummingbirds in the Andes are more endangered than other birds
choices.B: To explain how hummingbirds survive cold nights despite their high energy needs
choices.C: To compare the metabolism of hummingbirds with that of larger mammals
choices.D: To describe how researchers measure the heart rates of sleeping birds

candidates.explanation: The text sets up a problem (high energy use overnight), explains torpor as the solution, and adds a detail about how deep torpor can be.

A.rationale: Nothing in the text concerns endangerment.

strategy.explanation: Summarize the problem and the solution.

candidates.remember: Purpose questions ask what the whole text is trying to do.

candidates.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?

choices.A: each mole-rat's chirp pattern is determined entirely by the colony that it was born into.
choices.B: mole-rats cannot reliably tell their own colony's chirps apart from those of other colonies.
choices.C: removing a colony's queen causes the remaining mole-rats to stop chirping altogether.
choices.D: a colony's dialect is learned rather than inherited and may be held in place partly by the queen.

candidates.evidence: until a new queen took over and the calls grew similar again
candidates.explanation: The cross-fostering result shows dialects are learned; the queen-removal result shows they loosen without a queen and tighten under a new one.

A.rationale: Pups raised by another colony adopted that colony's dialect, not their birth colony's.

B.rationale: They respond more strongly to their own colony's dialect, so they can tell them apart.

C.rationale: The chirps became more varied, not silent.

hints: What do the two experiments each show?

strategy.explanation: Combine both findings before reading the choices.

candidates.remember: "These findings" means the answer must fit all of them.

candidates.stem: Which choice best describes data from the table that support the researchers' conclusion?

choices.A: The rate was 85% when an observer was visibly present but only 40% when sensors recorded it without an observer.
choices.B: The rate recorded by automated sensors at room entrances over the months with no observer present was 40%.
choices.C: The rate recorded over the same months when a trained observer was visibly present was 85%.
choices.D: Both methods recorded staff cleaning their hands at rates of at least 40% during the same months of the study.

candidates.evidence: rates recorded by visible observers likely overstate
candidates.explanation: The conclusion compares observed and unobserved rates; A shows 85% with an observer versus 40% without.

B.rationale: This gives only one method's rate and does not compare the two.

C.rationale: This gives only the observed rate, with nothing to compare it to.

D.rationale: This hides the gap between the methods, which is what the conclusion depends on.

hints: Which two conditions does the claim compare?

strategy.explanation: Find the comparison in the claim.

candidates.remember: A comparison claim needs data from both conditions.

candidates.subskill: Command of evidence: textual (supporting a hypothesis)
candidates.stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Vander Wall's hypothesis?

choices.A: Nutcrackers recovered a larger number of their caches in years when they had buried more pine seeds during the previous fall.
choices.B: Nutcrackers recovered seeds from their own caches far more often than from the caches made by other nutcrackers nearby.
choices.C: When nearby landmarks were all shifted 20 centimeters in one direction, the birds probed about 20 centimeters from their caches in that same direction.
choices.D: Seeds buried by nutcrackers sometimes sprouted into new pine trees whenever the birds failed to recover them the following spring.

candidates.evidence: by remembering the positions of nearby landmarks
candidates.explanation: If the birds rely on landmarks, moving the landmarks should move their searches by the same amount; C shows exactly that, which smell or random search cannot explain.

A.rationale: How many seeds were buried says nothing about how the birds find them.

B.rationale: This could be explained by smell or other cues as well as by landmarks.

D.rationale: This is about unrecovered seeds, not about how caches are found.

hints: What result would only landmark memory explain?

strategy.explanation: Ask what each finding rules out.

candidates.remember: The strongest support rules out the competing explanations.

candidates.stem: Based on the texts, how would Parker Pearson's team (Text 2) most likely respond to the argument in Text 1?

choices.A: By agreeing that glaciers carried the bluestones, since the team found no human activity in the Preseli Hills
choices.B: By arguing that evidence of quarrying at the source outcrops suggests that people removed the bluestones there and moved them
choices.C: By arguing that the bluestones actually came from quarries near Stonehenge rather than from Wales
choices.D: By suggesting that the bluestones were added to Stonehenge long after its larger stones were in place

candidates.evidence: found stone tools, wedges, and artificial platforms beneath the rock faces
candidates.explanation: Text 1 says glaciers moved the stones; Text 2's quarry tools, platforms, and stone-shaped gaps at the Welsh outcrops point to people extracting the stones there.

A.rationale: Text 2 reports tools, platforms, and hearths, which are signs of human activity.

C.rationale: Text 2's evidence is in the Preseli Hills in Wales, the same source Text 1 names.

D.rationale: Text 2 does not discuss the order in which the stones were placed.

hints: What does Text 2's evidence show happened at the source?

strategy.explanation: Identify each text's explanation for how the stones arrived.

candidates.remember: Cross-text answers must follow from the second text's evidence.

candidates.subskill: Rhetorical synthesis (emphasizing a source of an idea)
candidates.stem: The student wants to emphasize where Tu found the clue that led to her discovery. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?

choices.A: In 1969, Tu Youyou began searching for a new malaria treatment, and in 2015 she shared a Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for her discovery.
choices.B: Tu Youyou's team screened more than 2,000 traditional herbal remedies in its search for a new treatment for malaria.
choices.C: A 1,600-year-old text describing a cold-water preparation of sweet wormwood gave Tu Youyou the clue that led her to artemisinin.
choices.D: Extracting sweet wormwood at a low temperature preserved artemisinin, the active compound that Tu Youyou's team went on to discover.

candidates.evidence: A 1,600-year-old text described soaking sweet wormwood in cold water.
candidates.explanation: The goal is the source of the clue: the ancient text. Only C names it and connects it to the discovery.

A.rationale: This gives the start and the award but not where the clue came from.

B.rationale: This describes the search but not the specific source of the clue.

D.rationale: This explains the method but not where the idea for it came from.

hints: Which note names the source of the clue?

strategy.explanation: Match the goal to a single note, then check the choice.

candidates.remember: The goal tells you which information must appear.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?
candidates.evidence: Radiocarbon dating requires destroying a small sample
candidates.explanation: The first sentence lists drawbacks; the second says the method remains standard anyway. "Still" signals that concession.

A.rationale: The method's standard status is not a result of its drawbacks.

B.rationale: The second sentence is not an example of the drawbacks.

C.rationale: Remaining the standard is not similar to destroying samples or being slow.

hints: Does the method stay standard because of or despite its drawbacks?
candidates.remember: After listing drawbacks, a concession transition introduces the main point.

candidates.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
candidates.explanation: The past perfect is formed with "had" plus the past participle: "had written."

A.rationale: "Wrote" is the simple past; after "had," the past participle is needed.

C.rationale: "Had writing" is not a standard verb form.

candidates.remember: Had + past participle: had written, had gone, had chosen.

revision_log.reason: Both round-1 blind solves matched all keys with no blocking flags; both noted the Andes sentence in S037-03 simplified the study's finding about fat reserves. Replaced it with the recorded minimum torpor body temperature (about 3 degrees Celsius). The sentence is not tested by the item (key and evidence unchanged); not re-solved.
